'''James Richard "Jim" Jackson''' (May 16, 1924 – March 20, 2011) was an American [[mathematician]], well known for his contribution to [[queueing theory]].

Jackson was born in [[Denver]] and raised in [[Beverly Hills]].<ref name="laobit">{{cite web|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/latimes/obituary.aspx?pid=149856676|title=Obituary: James R. Jackson|work=Los Angeles Times|date=April 2, 2011}}</ref> He served in the [[United States Air Force]] during [[World War II]]. After his service, he earned an [[Bachelor of Arts|A.B.]] in 1946, an [[Master of Arts|M.A.]] in 1950 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1952, with a thesis titled ''Abstract Function Spaces and Their Homotopy Theory.''<ref name="mathgen" /> All of these degrees were from [[UCLA]] where Jackson remained in the [[UCLA Anderson School of Management|School of Management]] for his career until his retirement in 1985.<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: James R. Jackson|publisher=[[UCLA Anderson School of Management]]}}</ref>

While at [[University of California, Los Angeles]]  he developed the [[Jackson's theorem (queueing theory)|Jackson's theorem]] and some of the first models that could predict the performance of networks with several nodes. Jackson's work was inspired by his experience in the [[Los Angeles]] aircraft industry,<ref>{{cite journal|title=James R. Jackson|journal=Production and Operations Management|volume=17|issue=6|date=November–December 2008|pages=i–ii|doi=10.3401/poms.1080.0060|url=http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/poms.2008.17.issue-6/issuetoc|url-access=subscription}}</ref> but the results found applications in the design of computers, manufacturing and the then emerging [[packet switched network]]s, such as those undertaken by [[Leonard Kleinrock]] in 1961.<ref>{{cite journal|authorlink=Leonard Kleinrock|first=Leonard|last=Kleinrock|url=http://www.cs.ucla.edu/~lk/PS/paper221.pdf|title=Creating a mathematical theory of computer networks|journal=[[Operations Research (journal)|Operations Research]]|volume=50|number=1|pages=125–131|year=2002|doi=10.1287/opre.50.1.125.17772|jstor=3088461|doi-access=free}}</ref>

He spent his retirement in [[Tehachapi, California]].<ref name="laobit" />
